paras: The attempted lynching of Charles Jefferson took place in Washington County, Pennsylvania, at the end of January and start of February 1903, when crowds in several towns tried to seize Jefferson, a young Black man accused of assaulting the small daughter of Dr. George R. Conger of Taylorstown. Armed officers carried him through the crowds to the jail at Washington, Pa., and he was brought to trial on February 12. A Richmond paper used the episode to argue that lynching was no more a Southern practice than a Northern one.

According to a telegram from Washington, Pa., dated January 31, Jefferson was said to have been caught attempting an "indecent assault" on Dr. Conger's daughter, whose age it gave as two and a half. The same report said the doctor came off "worsted" in an encounter with the accused, who escaped and was hunted for several hours by officers and private citizens before word came at about 3 o'clock that he had been captured at West Alexander.

When a constable arrived to take Jefferson away, a large crowd gathered and threatened vengeance, and the officers, with drawn revolvers, fought their way through it to put him on a train. At Clayville, by the account of a Philadelphia Record correspondent, a mob of 300 men waited with a rope, but the car doors were locked and an officer with a revolver stood at each entrance, and the crowd was "cowed." Mobs formed in four towns in all, and a brief report credited "a strong body of constables" with saving his life.

The officers took Jefferson off the train at Taylorstown so that Dr. Conger could identify him, again forcing their way through a crowd to the Conger house. There, the correspondent wrote, Conger fired a revolver at the "cowering negro," and the shot missed his face by a few inches after an officer knocked the doctor's arm up. After the identification Jefferson was taken on to Washington, where a "hooting, threatening mob" followed him through the streets and he had to be carried the last few blocks, "completely overcome with terror."

An extra guard was placed on the jail because a demonstration by Taylorstown residents was expected. No arrest of any member of the crowds, or of Dr. Conger for the shot, appears in the coverage. Jefferson's trial on the assault charge opened on the afternoon of February 12 before Judge Taylor in a court room "filled almost to overflowing." A telegram from the trial reported that many persons thought "the colored boy" innocent and believed the doctor was taking revenge for earlier differences with him; no report of the verdict was found.

Only white papers carried the case, and the Black papers searched did not report it. The Wheeling Sunday Register's first telegram ran under the headline "Negro Fiend Caught at West Alexander" and stated the accusation as fact. The Alexandria Gazette's one-paragraph brief on February 2 called the offense a "criminal assault" on a 3-year-old and said "the little girl will die."

The Richmond Times Dispatch turned the story into an editorial, "The Same Everywhere," on February 4, setting the Pennsylvania mobs against the Rev. Dr. Charles H. Parkhurst's sermon that same Sunday on Southern "barbarism" toward Black people. The paper said it did "not justify or excuse lynching" but argued that wherever many Black people lived in the North, "the bad negro is summarily punished by the indignant whites." By contrast, the Wheeling Register's report from the trial on February 13 gave space to local doubt of the accused's guilt.

The reports differ on the child's age, giving two and a half years in the first telegram, three years in the Gazette brief and "not yet two" at the trial. They also differ on the charge, from an attempted "indecent assault" in the local telegrams to a "criminal assault" that would prove fatal in the Gazette, a claim the later trial report does not repeat. Two papers date the lynching attempts to Sunday, February 1, while the Washington telegram places the capture on the afternoon of Saturday, January 31.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Charles Jefferson
bases: Crowds and a mob of 300 with a rope tried repeatedly to seize and lynch Jefferson while officers took him to jail, and failed (A3, A4).

Jefferson was not killed; he was jailed and brought to trial alive (A3, A4, A5). The mobs, one of 300 men with a rope, sought to lynch him for the accused assault, which makes this an attempted lynching (A3, A4).

A Washington, Pa., telegram (A1, A2), a news brief (A3) and a Philadelphia Record correspondent quoted in an editorial (A4) independently report the accusation, the capture and the mobs, and a later telegram reports the trial (A5).

accounts.label: Washington, Pa., telegram
accounts.gist: A 'negro fiend' was caught attempting an indecent assault on Dr. Conger's daughter, fought with the doctor, escaped, and was captured at West Alexander after a manhunt.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: Repeated attempts were made to lynch Jefferson at four towns after a 'criminal assault' on the child, who 'will die'; constables saved him.

accounts.label: Philadelphia Record correspondent
accounts.gist: Officers with drawn revolvers fought through crowds, kept a mob of 300 with a rope out of the locked car at Clayville, and stopped Dr. Conger's shot at Taylorstown before Jefferson was jailed.

accounts.label: Washington, Pa., trial telegram
accounts.gist: At the trial many persons thought the boy innocent and the doctor bent on revenge over earlier differences.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Sunday Register headlined 'Negro Fiend Caught at West Alexander' and presented the accusation as fact.
The Alexandria Gazette ran a one-paragraph brief stating the 'criminal assault' as fact and crediting the constables with saving his life.

The Times Dispatch said it did 'not justify or excuse lynching' but used the episode to argue the North was no better than the South and that 'the bad negro is summarily punished by the indignant whites.'
The Wheeling Register's trial report reported local doubt of the accused's guilt.

conflicts.note: The local telegrams (A1, A5) are closer to the source than the brief (A3).

versions.value: 'indecent assault', with many believing him innocent and the doctor seeking revenge

conflicts.note: The brief's graver charge and claim that the child would die are not repeated in the trial report twelve days later.

versions.value: capture on the afternoon of January 31 (Saturday)

conflicts.note: The correspondent says Jefferson was 'brought here this evening' after the capture, which may place the train journey on January 31; the papers do not settle it.
The editorial's own quotation has Jefferson taken off at Taylorstown for identification and then brought on to the jail, so 'Taylorstown' in its lead-in appears to be an error.

record_check.dossier: Accused of an (attempted) indecent assault on Dr. Conger's daughter, age given as under two to three; 'criminal assault' is one brief's wording
Threats and a mob with a rope during transport, plus a revolver shot by Dr. Conger that missed; no jail siege is reported, only an expected demonstration
Unnamed crowds (one of 300 at Clayville) and Dr. George R. Conger, who fired at Jefferson
The Parkhurst link is the Richmond editorial's framing, not part of the event; the summary omits Conger's shot, the trial on February 12 and local doubts of guilt
Four white reports (five article blocks) found; no Black-press coverage found
